assessed
  • asymmetry — Across all four cancellation-flow retention screens (steps 10, 11, 12, 13), the "keep" option is a large, solid, brand-colored (mustard/gold) pill button while the "cancel" option is rendered as small, plain underlined gray text beneath it. The measured area_ratio is ~13x (step 10/11) and ~12x (step 12/13) in favor of the positive/keep option, font_size_ratio is ~1.6x larger for keep, and the keep button sits ~84px above the cancel link (vertical_position_delta_px -84), giving it top billing as well. This is visually confirmed in the screenshots: the "Yes, keep my 50% off plan" and "Keep my membership" buttons are bold, filled, large rounded buttons dominating the center of the page, while "no thanks, cancel anyway" / "yes, cancel my membership" are small underlined text links with no button styling, positioned directly below and clearly de-emphasized. This is a textbook, strongly intentional asymmetry between the accept (keep subscription) and reject (cancel) choices in the core cancellation flow, appearing consistently across the two retention offer screens the user must pass through to cancel. The newsletter popup at step 1 also shows moderate asymmetry (area_ratio 2.5, contrast_ratio ~4.1) but the cancellation-flow instances are far more extreme and directly relevant to the goal-blocking pattern.
  • covertness — Across the retention/cancellation steps (10-13), the "no thanks, cancel anyway" / "yes, cancel my membership" option is consistently rendered as a plain underlined text link directly beneath a large, high-contrast colored button (the accept/keep option). This is a clear case of visual de-emphasis (asymmetry): smaller font, no button styling, lower position, higher tab order — all captured in the visual_asymmetry evidence (area_ratio ~12-13x, font_size_ratio ~1.6x, negative always below the positive). However, the reject option is never hidden behind a secondary click, collapsed menu, tooltip, mislabeled control, tiny icon, or placed off in an unrelated part of the page — it is fully visible, legibly labeled with its actual function ("cancel anyway," "cancel my membership"), immediately adjacent to the primary button, and always present without scrolling or extra interaction. Screenshots (steps 10-13) show the link in plain, readable text directly under the highlighted button, not disguised as something else (e.g., not styled to look like a disclaimer, footer note, or unrelated element) and not visually camouflaged into the background. This pattern matches asymmetry (reduced prominence) rather than covertness (deliberate concealment/disguise). There is no evidence of the negative option being mislabeled, hidden in a menu, buried in unrelated text, or rendered in low-contrast/matching-background color that would suggest intentional concealment beyond simple de-emphasis. Given the evidence available is only the asymmetry metrics plus screenshots showing a legible, clearly-labeled link, I judge this does not meet the bar for covertness as distinct from asymmetry.
  • deception — The click at step 13 on "yes, cancel my membership" recorded network_fired=false and route_changed=false, which the code agent flagged as a claimed state-change action that produced no observable effect. However, the very next recorded step (14), on an apparently identical click of the same selector/button, does show network_fired=true, route_changed=true, and lands on a "Membership cancelled" confirmation screen with an explicit "won't be charged again" claim. This pattern is consistent with a user needing to click the link twice (e.g. first click may have been swallowed by a modal/notification prompt overlay visible in the screenshots, or a double-render/hydration delay) rather than a structural contradiction where the cancellation is claimed to succeed but silently doesn't. Since the flow does eventually deliver a real network-backed cancellation and confirmation page, there isn't clear evidence that the FINAL claimed action failed to do what it said. But the isolated network-inert click at step 13 is still an unexplained discrepancy between an apparent UI action and no backend effect, which could itself be read as deceptive (button appeared clickable/actionable but did nothing) if it wasn't just a duplicate/redundant registration of the same click. Given the ambiguity -- one non-firing click sandwiched between two firing ones for the same claimed action -- I can't be fully confident this is a genuine 'claimed action did nothing' deception instance versus a benign double-click/logging artifact of the recorder. This warrants 'unsure' rather than a confident 'fires' at low severity, since severity/confidence here is speculative without clearer signal that the site intentionally presented a broken cancel button as functional.
  • information_hiding — The signup screen (step 4/5) discloses upfront, in visible copy beneath the CTA, that "After your 30-day trial, your card will be automatically charged ₹499/month until you cancel. Cancel anytime from Account settings." This is the price/term that governs the whole subscription, and it is shown before the user commits (clicks "Start My Free Trial"), not hidden until later. The cancellation flow itself (steps 7-17) does not reveal any new fee, condition, or term that was withheld earlier — it shows a retention offer (50% off, ₹249.50/month) which is an alternative offer, not a previously-hidden cost, and the price_drift evidence shows a decrease (from 12999 to 249.5) reflecting the discount branch price, not a hidden charge sprung on the user. There is no evidence of a fee, cancellation deadline, proration, or penalty condition that was concealed during signup and only surfaced during cancellation. The retention offer's discounted price is clearly stated at the point it is offered, not hidden. Given the definition requires a cost/term withheld from the user until later, and here the core recurring fee and cancellation terms were disclosed at signup time, this attribute does not fire. I have moderate-high confidence there's no hidden term, though I can't fully rule out something outside the visible screenshots (e.g., other T&Cs), hence not full confidence.
